insights.title: A material that cannot burn downward on Earth can burn steadily in microgravity
insights.text: In BASS, a fabric that only sputters and goes out when burning downward in 1 g kept burning against the airflow in microgravity until the fuel was used up. Without buoyancy the flame is not blown off, so passing a 1 g test does not prove a material is safe in orbit.

citations.quote: this fuel will support opposed-flow burning in microgravity
the normal-gravity, downward-burning flame is ignited, but sputters and then goes out

insights.title: NASA's 1 g material screening test may not be conservative for space
insights.text: Spacecraft materials are selected with NASA-STD-6001 Test 1, an upward-burning test in 1 g. BASS-II was built to test whether ventilated materials burn as well or better in microgravity, and NASA's Researcher's Guide notes drop-tower results suggesting Test 1 might not be conservative.

citations.quote: it may not be conservative for flammability in space
segregates material based on 1-g behavior without consideration of low gravity effects
recent drop-tower results suggest that the current Test 1 might not be conservative

insights.title: Cabin ventilation speed decides whether a microgravity flame lives or dies
insights.text: In microgravity the only oxygen supply is the forced airflow, and flames are very sensitive to it. A low-flow 'quenching' extinction limit exists that can only be observed in microgravity, because on Earth buoyancy always adds about 20 cm/s of flow. Shutting off fans is a real fire-control lever.

citations.quote: The flames in microgravity are very sensitive to flow speed
The observation of the quenching extinction branch is only possible at microgravity
Normal gravity studies are limited to flow speeds above the minimum buoyant speed in the flame zone (20 cm/s for this system)

insights.title: Saffire measured how fast a large fire grows in a real spacecraft
insights.text: Saffire I–III burned large fabric and plastic samples inside an uncrewed Cygnus cargo vehicle after it left the ISS, at 20–30 cm/s airflow, to find out how quickly a large-scale fire grows in low gravity and whether it settles to a steady spread rate.

citations.quote: determine how rapidly a large-scale fire grows in low-gravity and whether it reaches a steady-state spread rate
the experiments were conducted at a flow velocity of 30 cm/s compared to 20 cm/s during Saffire I

insights.title: Smoke detectors for spacecraft can't be designed from 1 g smoke data
insights.text: Without buoyant mixing, smoke stays near its source longer, and SAME was designed around the hypothesis that this grows larger particles than in 1 g. Its final report concludes that direct low-g particle data, not extrapolation from 1 g, is needed to design spacecraft smoke detectors.

citations.quote: will lead to larger particles compared to those produced in 1g
as opposed to extrapolation from 1-g data, direct knowledge of low-g combustion particulate is needed for more confident design of smoke detectors for spacecraft

insights.title: Detector principle matters: ionization saw every SAME smoke, light scattering missed some
insights.text: In SAME, the ionization-type Space Shuttle detector gave strong signals in all tests, while light-scattering detection was less effective for some Teflon tests, whose smoke had few large particles. Detector choice should match the smoke of the materials actually on board.

citations.quote: All of the tests conducted in this series of experiments showed strong signals on the Space Shuttle detector (ionization)
which was seen for some of the Teflon tests

insights.title: In orbit, dust stays airborne — a false-alarm risk for smoke detectors
insights.text: DAFT found more large dust particles on orbit than on the ground, because nothing makes them settle. Detectors in a weightless (or dusty lunar) cabin must tell smoke from dust; DAFT adapted a TSI P-Trak particle counter to microgravity to measure this.

citations.quote: without gravity to drive settling, more of the larger particles from the dust sample should remain entrained
TSI P-Trak was modified for use in microgravity

insights.title: FLEX mapped the oxygen level below which a flame can't survive, by pressure and suppressant
insights.text: FLEX burned heptane and methanol droplets on the ISS to find the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) as a function of pressure and of the suppressant gas added (CO2, helium). This is the number an engineer needs to size an extinguishing system.

citations.quote: A primary objective of the experiments is to determine the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) as a function of ambient pressure and determine how the presence of a suppressant influences the LOI

insights.title: BASS tested nitrogen, the agent planned for future spacecraft extinguishers
insights.text: BASS used nitrogen as a flame suppressant on burning solids in microgravity, giving a direct link to current and planned extinguishment techniques.

citations.quote: Using nitrogen as a flame suppressant in microgravity provides a direct link to current and planned extinguishment techniques

insights.title: Heptane droplets burned to completion at only 14% O2
insights.text: In the FLEX table, the lowest O2 at which a heptane droplet burned completely was 14% (at 102 kPa), well below normal air. Flame extinction was recorded from 12% up to 30% O2 across 186 tests, depending on fuel, droplet size and diluent. Lowering O2 to ~15–17% is not by itself enough to guarantee a liquid-fuel fire goes out.

insights.title: Less oxygen makes droplet flames go out sooner — about 0.11 mm per O2 point
insights.text: A linear model fitted to 188 FLEX tests (cross-validated R² 0.72) shows the flame goes out at a 0.11 mm larger droplet diameter for every 1 percentage point less O2, with fuel, pressure, CO2/He and initial size held fixed. Use `ai.model.predict_flex` within the tested ranges only.

insights.title: Saffire-II recorded spread rates of 2.1–2.6 mm/s
insights.text: Only 2 of the Saffire-II table rows carry a flame spread rate (2.1–2.6 mm/s at ~22% O2, 20 cm/s flow; materials: Cotton-Fiberglass (SIBAL)). The full image-derived results are in the Saffire MergeResult spreadsheets on PSI.

insights.title: No solid-material test at the O2 level of Lunar base (30 % O2, 70.3 kPa).
insights.text: 47 tests near this atmosphere, by fuel phase {'solid': 0, 'droplet': 41, 'gas': 6} (only droplets and gas flames); 0 solid-fuel rows within ±6 percentage points of O2 even ignoring pressure. Solids (fabrics, plastics) are the main fire load in a habitat. Closest proxy: ACME BRE (PSI-20) - a gas burner that emulates burning solids - ran at 21–40 % O2 (17 of 18 test days whose O2 range reaches 30 % ±6 points); its pressures are not in the table.

insights.title: Solid materials were tested only up to 22.2 % O2, below every planned exploration atmosphere (30–34 % O2).
insights.text: 143 O2 values in 3 solid-fuel investigations with an O2 column; range 13.6–22.2 %. The BASS (PSI-26) table records no O2 at all. insights.title: No solid-material test has a recorded pressure in the PSI tables.
insights.text: 0 of 380 solid-fuel rows have a pressure value (BASS, BASS-II, SAFFIRE and SAME tables have no pressure column).

insights.title: No partial-gravity (Moon 1/6 g, Mars 3/8 g) combustion data in PSI.
insights.text: All 19 flight investigations ran in microgravity; ACME E-FIELD (PSI-22) uses electric fields only as a proxy. Microgravity and 1 g results bound partial-g behaviour.

insights.title: Nothing was tested at spacesuit conditions (100 % O2, 29.6 kPa).
insights.text: Highest O2 in any test: 85 % (inverse gas flames, PSI-10 / PSI-159); 0 tests near spacesuit conditions.

insights.title: No droplet-extinction data at exploration-atmosphere pressure
insights.text: FLEX never went below about 70 kPa, so its extinction results cannot be applied directly to the 56.5 kPa exploration atmosphere planned for Moon/Mars habitats and rovers; the FLEX model refuses to predict there (pressure_kPa=56.5 is outside the FLEX range for heptane (70.394–207.156) — not extrapolating)
